disclaimer: This knowledge base is for informational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Always consult a registered tax agent or the ATO directly.

chunks.title: Gym Memberships - General Rule
chunks.content: Gym memberships are generally NOT deductible for most Australian taxpayers. The ATO takes the view that maintaining general fitness and health is a private expense. However, exceptions exist for employees whose job specifically requires a high level of physical fitness, such as police officers, firefighters, defence force personnel, and professional athletes. A fitness instructor or personal trainer who uses the gym to train clients (not for personal training) may also have a partial deduction. The nexus between the expense and income-earning activities must be direct and demonstrable. Simply working in an office and wanting to stay healthy does not make a gym membership deductible. ATO ID 2007/182 confirms that gym expenses for a taxpayer whose job does not specifically require physical fitness are private in nature.
evidence_required: employment contract confirming physical fitness requirement

chunks.title: Personal Trainer Fees
chunks.content: Personal trainer fees follow the same rules as gym memberships. They are private expenses unless your employment specifically requires a high level of physical fitness. Police officers who are required by their employer to maintain fitness levels may claim PT fees. Professional athletes training under a structured program directly tied to income-earning activities may claim fees. A casual employee who gets a PT to 'feel better at work' cannot claim the expense. The expense must have a sufficient connection to the production of assessable income. There must be a direct and proximate relationship between the personal training and your income-producing activities.
who_can_claim: fitness coaches training for competition income
who_cannot_claim: employees seeking performance improvement not required by employer

chunks.title: Supplements and Nutrition Products
chunks.content: Supplements such as protein powders, creatine, vitamins, and other nutritional products are almost always treated as private expenses by the ATO. Even for professional athletes and fitness professionals, the ATO generally disallows these deductions because they are considered maintenance of personal health rather than directly related to income-producing activities. The few exceptions would be supplements prescribed by a medical practitioner or dietitian as treatment for a specific work-related condition, or supplements explicitly required under a contract of employment with direct nexus to income. General health supplements bought from chemists or supplement stores are non-deductible.
who_can_claim: professional athletes (very limited, with medical prescription)
under specific contractual requirements with documented evidence

chunks.title: Fitness Equipment - General Employees
chunks.ato_reference: Section 8-1, Division 40 ITAA 1997; ATO Depreciation rules
chunks.content: Fitness equipment purchased for home or personal use is generally not deductible. The ATO requires a direct connection to income production. However, for fitness instructors, personal trainers, or coaches who use equipment to train clients and generate income, the equipment may be deductible. Items under $300 can be claimed immediately; items over $300 must be depreciated over the effective life. If equipment is used for both work and personal purposes, only the work-use percentage is deductible. A fitness instructor who uses a treadmill only for client sessions can claim it; one who also uses it personally must apportion.
who_can_claim: personal trainers using equipment for client sessions
who_cannot_claim: general employees buying home gym equipment for personal health
evidence_required: percentage of work vs personal use

chunks.title: Fitness Equipment - Professional Athletes
chunks.content: Professional athletes can deduct the cost of sport-specific equipment used to generate income. This includes equipment directly used in competition or training for competition. A professional footballer can claim boots, mouthguards, and protective equipment. A professional swimmer can claim goggles, swim caps, and training gear. Equipment that crosses over into personal use must be apportioned. The ATO looks at whether the activity is a business/income-earning activity versus a hobby. Amateur athletes and serious amateurs cannot claim equipment because their sporting activity is not income-producing.
who_can_claim: professional athletes earning income from sport

chunks.title: Activewear and Sports Clothing
chunks.content: Activewear and sports clothing are generally private expenses. The ATO only allows deductions for clothing that is a compulsory uniform, occupation-specific clothing not suitable for everyday wear, or protective clothing. General activewear such as yoga pants, running shoes, gym shorts, and sports bras cannot be claimed even if worn exclusively for work-related exercise. However, a fitness instructor whose employer mandates a specific branded uniform (not just generic activewear) may claim the uniform. Protective sports equipment (helmet, shin pads, mouthguard) may be deductible for professional athletes. TR 98/5 is the key ruling on work-related clothing.
who_can_claim: employees with employer-mandated specific uniform (not generic activewear)
who_cannot_claim: people buying activewear for gym or personal exercise
evidence_required: employer uniform policy confirming compulsory nature
logo/branding evidence if claimed as uniform

chunks.title: Fitness Instructors - Deductible Expenses
chunks.ato_reference: Section 8-1 ITAA 1997; ATO Occupational Guide - Fitness Instructors
chunks.content: Fitness instructors and personal trainers have expanded deduction rights compared to general employees. They can generally claim: (1) Gym fees for facilities where they teach or train clients, (2) Equipment used exclusively or primarily for client training, (3) First aid courses and CPR certificates required for work, (4) Professional development courses (fitness certifications, CECs), (5) Professional association fees (Fitness Australia, AUSACTIVE), (6) Work-related clothing that is a required specific uniform, (7) Equipment depreciation if over $300, (8) Work-related phone calls and internet for client management. They cannot claim: personal training for their own fitness, supplements for personal use, general activewear.
specific_deductions: Gym hire fees for client sessions
evidence_required: diary of work vs personal use for equipment

chunks.title: Professional Athletes - Deductible Expenses
chunks.ato_reference: Section 8-1 ITAA 1997; ATO Publication - Professional Sportspeople
chunks.content: Professional athletes earning income from their sport can deduct a wide range of expenses. Deductible items include: sport-specific equipment and gear, travel to competitions and training, physiotherapy and sports medicine (if work-related), coaching and training fees directly related to competition income, agent fees, promotional costs, and occupation-specific clothing (competition uniforms). The ATO distinguishes professional athletes (income-earning) from serious amateurs (hobby). Income must be material and the activity must be conducted with business-like approach. See the ATO's dedicated guide for professional sportspeople.
specific_deductions: Travel to competitions and training camps

chunks.title: Police, Military and Emergency Services - Fitness Expenses
chunks.content: Police officers, military personnel, and certain emergency services workers can claim gym and fitness expenses where their employer requires them to maintain a specific level of physical fitness as a condition of employment. The key test is whether the employer mandates fitness tests or standards (e.g., police fitness tests, military PT requirements). If passing fitness tests is a condition of keeping your job, then reasonable gym and fitness expenses have a sufficient nexus to your income. ATO ID 2005/196 confirms police officers can claim gym fees where fitness testing is a job requirement. A letter or policy document from the employer confirming the fitness requirement is essential evidence.
who_can_claim: police officers with mandatory fitness testing
evidence_required: employer letter confirming mandatory fitness requirement

chunks.title: Sports Associations and Club Fees
chunks.content: Membership fees for sports clubs and associations are generally private expenses. The fact that you network at the club or that fitness helps your work performance is insufficient to make the fees deductible. Exceptions: A professional athlete whose primary income is from a sport may deduct club fees directly related to their income-earning competitions. A sports official or coach earning income from a specific sport may deduct the relevant association registration fee. General memberships at social sports clubs remain non-deductible even if they provide some fitness benefit.
evidence_required: evidence of income from the sport

chunks.title: Fitness Apps and Online Subscriptions
chunks.content: Fitness tracking apps and subscriptions are generally private expenses. However, fitness professionals (personal trainers, coaches) may claim subscriptions to client management software, programming tools (TrueCoach, PT Distinction), and professional development platforms. Personal fitness apps like Strava, MyFitnessPal, or Headspace used for personal health are not deductible. A sports coach who uses a video analysis app directly for client work may be able to claim it. The key test is whether the subscription is used for income-earning activities versus personal use.
who_can_claim: fitness professionals using apps for client management or programming
sports coaches using performance analysis tools
who_cannot_claim: individuals using apps for personal fitness tracking

chunks.title: Physiotherapy and Sports Medicine
chunks.content: Physiotherapy and sports medicine costs are generally private medical expenses and are not tax deductible (they may qualify for the private health insurance rebate instead). Exceptions exist for professional athletes and some emergency services workers where injury and treatment is a direct consequence of income-earning activities. A professional athlete recovering from a sports injury that occurred during a paid competition may deduct physiotherapy costs. The injury must be work-related, not arising from personal recreational activity. General sports massage for personal wellbeing or preventive care is a private expense.
who_can_claim: employees with workplace injury (workers' compensation scenario)
who_cannot_claim: general employees seeking sports massage for personal wellness
evidence_required: evidence linking injury to income-earning activity

chunks.title: First Aid and CPR Certification
chunks.ato_reference: Section 8-1 ITAA 1997; ATO Guide - Self-Education Expenses
chunks.content: First aid and CPR certification costs are deductible when required as a condition of your employment or directly related to your current income-earning activities. Fitness instructors, personal trainers, lifeguards, childcare workers, and others who are required to hold current first aid certification as part of their job can claim these costs. The renewal cost (typically every 3 years for first aid, every year for CPR) is also deductible if the certification is required for your current role. Note: If you obtain first aid certification to enter a new profession (not your current one), it may not be deductible.
who_can_claim: teachers with mandatory first aid requirements
evidence_required: evidence that certification is required for current employment

chunks.title: Fitness Certifications and Professional Development
chunks.content: Fitness certifications and professional development costs are deductible for current fitness professionals maintaining or upgrading skills used in their existing role. A personal trainer renewing their Cert IV in Fitness or completing CECs (Continuing Education Credits) required by Fitness Australia/AUSACTIVE can claim the cost. A fitness instructor undertaking specialty certifications (yoga, pilates, kettlebell) that expand their current service offering can generally claim these costs. Costs of initial qualifications to enter the fitness industry for the first time are NOT deductible (they are capital or private). ATO ID 2011/67 provides guidance on self-education expenses.
who_can_claim: instructors adding certifications to existing role
who_cannot_claim: people studying fitness to enter the industry for the first time

chunks.title: General Health Expenses - Private in Nature
chunks.content: General health and wellness expenses are private in nature and not deductible regardless of any indirect benefit to your work performance. The ATO's position is that maintaining general health is a personal responsibility. This includes: general yoga or pilates classes attended for personal wellbeing, naturopathy or dietitian services not related to a work injury, wellness apps and subscriptions for personal use, mental health apps (though some employer-reimbursed programs may be differently treated), and general preventive health spending. The argument that being healthier makes you more productive at work is specifically rejected by the ATO as insufficient nexus.
chunks.ato_note: Even where health maintenance indirectly benefits work performance, the ATO considers these expenses private unless there is a direct, specific nexus to income production.

chunks.title: Sporting Goods Stores - What You Can and Cannot Claim
chunks.content: Purchases from sporting goods stores are evaluated based on what was bought, not where it was purchased. The same rules apply: professional athletes can claim sport-specific equipment, fitness instructors can claim equipment used for client training, police and military can claim items required for mandatory fitness tests. But most purchases from sporting goods stores (running shoes for personal exercise, general activewear, personal fitness equipment) are private expenses. When buying from a sporting goods store as a fitness professional, keep itemised receipts and note the work purpose of each item.
evidence_required: itemised receipt showing specific items purchased

chunks.title: Wearable Fitness Technology (Garmin, Apple Watch, Fitbit)
chunks.content: Wearable fitness technology such as GPS watches, heart rate monitors, and fitness trackers are generally private expenses. However, they may be deductible for professional athletes who use them specifically for training data relevant to competition, or for fitness professionals who use them in the delivery of client services (e.g., a running coach using GPS data during client sessions). If the device is used for both work and personal purposes, the work-use percentage must be calculated. Devices over $300 must be depreciated. An Apple Watch used partly for fitness tracking and partly as a general smartwatch would require careful apportionment.
evidence_required: diary of work vs personal use
